You are reverse-engineering a C++ library PURELY AS A BLACK BOX by running a compiled binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test16_executable
Its C++ driver source is (library source is NOT available - do not look for it):

  int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
      if (argc < 2) return 1;
      std::string url = argv[1];
      std::cout << url_parser::URL::is_valid_url(url) << std::endl;       // LINE 1
      url_parser::URL parser(url);
      std::cout << url_parser::is_scheme_valid(parser.scheme()) << std::endl;  // LINE 2
      std::cout << url_parser::is_host_valid(parser.host()) << std::endl;      // LINE 3
      std::cout << url_parser::is_port_valid(parser.port()) << std::endl;      // LINE 4
      auto path_segments = url_parser::split_path(parser.path());
      std::cout << path_segments.size() << std::endl;                          // LINE 5
      for (const auto& segment : path_segments) std::cout << segment << std::endl;  // LINES 6+
      return 0;
  }

So each run gives you exactly 5 numbers + the path segments. Lines 1-4 are bools printed as 1/0.

KNOWN INTERFACE (from the binary's symbol table - this is all you get):
  namespace url_parser {
    std::string url_decode(const std::string&);
    std::string url_encode(const std::string&);
    std::vector<std::string> split_path(const std::string&);
    bool is_scheme_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_host_valid(const std::string&);
    bool is_port_valid(int);                 // NOTE: port is an int
    static bool URL::is_valid_url(const std::string&);
    class URL {
      URL(); URL(const std::string&);
      void parse(const std::string&);
      std::string scheme() const; std::string userinfo() const; std::string host() const;
      int port() const; std::string path() const; std::string query() const;
      std::string fragment() const; std::string authority() const;
      bool has_scheme/has_authority/has_userinfo/has_host/has_port/has_path/has_query/has_fragment() const;
      bool is_valid() const;
      ... setters, normalize(), normalize_case(), normalize_path(), normalize_query(), to_string(), operator==
    };
    // internal statics: trim(const std::string&), to_lower(const std::string&),
    //                   is_hex(char), hex_to_char(char)
    // to_lower is implemented as std::transform with a lambda taking (unsigned char)
  }

PROBE HARNESS - use this pattern (handles quoting safely):
  BIN=/workspace/dataset/test16_executable
  probe() { printf '%s => ' "$(printf '%q' "$1")"; "$BIN" "$1" 2>&1 | tr '\n' '|'; printf ' (exit %s)\n' "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; }
  probe 'http://example.com'
  probe $'http://a\tb'        # use $'...' for control chars / tabs / newlines
  probe "$(printf 'http://a\xc3\xa9')"   # for high bytes / UTF-8

You may run HUNDREDS of probes - do it in batches inside one bash call using loops. Be exhaustive and systematic:
sweep single characters, boundary lengths, every ASCII code 0..127 where relevant, high bytes 128..255,
empty strings, and combinations. Isolate one variable at a time.

ESTABLISHED FACTS (already confirmed, do not re-derive, but you MAY correct them if you find contradictions):
  ''                              => 0 0 0 0 0
  'http://example.com'            => 1 1 1 0 0
  'https://localhost:8080'        => 1 1 1 1 0

  'HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B'        => 1 1 1 0 2 [A,B]  (NO case normalization in parse)

  'http://[::1]:8080/x'           => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]  (!! port INVALID but host VALID - investigate)
  'http://[::1]/x'                => 1 1 1 0 1 [x]
  'http://ex ample.com'           => 1 1 0 0 0
  ':'                             => 1 0 0 0 1 [:]
  '://'                           => 0 0 0 0 0

=== YOUR ASSIGNMENT: ADVERSARIALLY REFUTE A PROPOSED RULE ===

Another engineer probed the binary and proposed this rule for "CLI contract and exact output formatting":

----- PROPOSED RULE -----
PROGRAM I/O CONTRACT (byte-exact, verified by hexdump)

1) ARGUMENT HANDLING
- Let argc be the raw process argument count (including argv[0]).
- if argc < 2  (i.e. no arguments after the program name, or even argc==0 via execve with an empty argv):
    write NOTHING to stdout, NOTHING to stderr, exit status 1.
- if argc >= 2: use argv[1] verbatim as the URL string. argv[2..] are read but never used and never affect
  output; exit status 0. (Confirmed with 2, 3, 51 and 1001 arguments.)
- argv[1] == "" (empty string) is a normal input, NOT the no-arg case: prints "0\n0\n0\n0\n0\n", exit 0.
  It does not fall through to a later non-empty argument.
- No option parsing whatsoever. "-h", "--help", "--version", "-v", "-", "--", "---" are treated as ordinary
  URL strings (e.g. "--help" -> "1\n0\n0\n0\n1\n--help\n").
- The argument is an ordinary NUL-terminated C string, so a NUL byte can never appear in the input; every other
  byte 0x01..0xFF is accepted verbatim (no validation, no transcoding, no locale/encoding sensitivity).
- Max testable argument length is the Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN limit of 131072 bytes: 131071-byte args work
  perfectly (exit 0, complete output); 131072+ is rejected by the kernel (E2BIG) before the program runs, so
  no program-side length limit is observable. No truncation, no crash at 131071 bytes.

2) STDOUT FORMAT  (this is the ENTIRE output; there is nothing else)
   line 1: is_valid_url(url)          -> exactly one byte '1' (0x31) or '0' (0x30), then LF
   line 2: is_scheme_valid(scheme)    -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 3: is_host_valid(host)        -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 4: is_port_valid(port)        -> '1' or '0', then LF
   line 5: N = path_segments.size()   -> plain unsigned decimal ASCII, no sign, no '+', no leading zeros
                                         (except the value 0 itself printed as "0"), no thousands separators,
                                         no padding, no spaces; then LF
   lines 6..5+N: each path segment, raw bytes exactly as stored, then LF.
- Bools use the default C++ numeric form (no boolalpha): never "true"/"false", never uppercase, never padded.
- Separator/terminator is always a single LF (0x0A). Never CR, never CRLF. No BOM. No leading/trailing spaces.
  A trailing LF is ALWAYS present after the last line (std::endl). Total output for argc>=2 therefore always
  ends with 0x0A and always contains at least 5 LFs.
- Exact byte count of stdout for argc>=2:
      total_bytes = 8 + (number of decimal digits in N) + 1 + sum over segments of (len(segment) + 1)
  Verified: 'http://example.com' -> 10 bytes; 'http://example.com/a/b/c' -> 16 bytes;
  1234 segments of length 3 -> 8 + 5 + 1234*4 = 4949 bytes (actual 4949).
- Segments are printed RAW and unescaped/undecoded. If a segment contains an LF byte, the output becomes
  ambiguous (a "segment" spans two output lines). Therefore line count == 5 + N only when no segment contains
  an LF. Example: $'http://ex.com/a\nb/c' -> "1\n1\n1\n0\n2\na\nb\nc\n" (6 physical lines, N=2; segment 1 is
  "a\nb", segment 2 is "c"). TAB (0x09), CR (0x0D), VT, FF, space (0x20), 0x7F and all high bytes 0x80..0xFF
  pass through byte-for-byte inside segments; there is no quoting, escaping, percent-decoding, or trimming.
- Empty segments are never printed (they are dropped before printing), so no output line among 6..5+N is ever
  a bare LF unless the segment itself literally contains an LF.
- A segment never contains '/' (0x2F).

3) STDERR
- Never written to, for any input. Verified 0 bytes of stderr across ~1800 probes: every single byte 0x01-0xFF
  as the whole argument, as a host character, and as a path character; 500 random 60-byte urandom strings;
  400 structured token-fuzz URLs; port values 2147483648, 4294967296, 99999999999999999999, -2147483649 and a
  5000-digit port (no std::stoi out_of_range escapes -> library catches it; no "terminate called ..." message,
  no SIGABRT/exit 134 ever observed).

4) EXIT STATUS
- 1  : argc < 2 (no output at all).
- 0  : every other case, for every input tested, including empty string, control bytes, invalid UTF-8,
       131071-byte arguments, 65526 path segments, and port overflow.
- 141 (SIGPIPE, 128+13): only when the reader closes the pipe early (e.g. `| head -1`) while the program still
  has lines to write. Output is flushed line-by-line (std::endl), so this is reachable for outputs of >= ~3
  lines; a 12-byte output typically finishes first and yields 0 (race).
- Writing to a failing stdout is silently ignored: `>/dev/full` gives exit 0 with empty stderr (stream error
  state is never checked). Closed stdout (`>&-`) also gives exit 0, silently.

5) NON-INFLUENCES (all verified)
- stdin is never read (piping data in or /dev/null changes nothing).
- Environment is irrelevant: `env -i`, LANG/LC_ALL/LC_NUMERIC = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, POSIX,
  invalid_LOCALE all give identical bytes; line 5 is never locale-grouped (12345 stays "12345").
- argv[0] value/path is irrelevant (renaming the binary changes nothing).
- Fully deterministic: 30 identical runs of a complex URL produce identical md5.
- The program itself emits LF only; the CR seen under a pty (`script`) is the terminal's ONLCR translation,
  not program output.

RUST-IMPLEMENTABLE PSEUDOCODE
  let args: Vec<OsString> = env::args_os().collect();      // args[0] is program name
  if args.len() < 2 { exit(1); }                            // nothing printed
  let url: &[u8] = args[1].as_bytes();
  let u = URL::parse(url);
  let mut out = Vec::new();
  out.extend(if URL::is_valid_url(url) {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_scheme_valid(u.scheme) {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_host_valid(u.host)     {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  out.extend(if is_port_valid(u.port)     {b"1\n"} else {b"0\n"});
  let segs = split_path(u.path);
  out.extend(format!("{}\n", segs.len()).as_bytes());       // usize, plain decimal
  for s in &segs { out.extend(s); out.push(b'\n'); }        // raw bytes
  stdout().write_all(&out) (ignore errors); exit(0);
-------------------------

They flagged these uncertainties:
  - Arguments longer than 131071 bytes cannot be delivered on Linux (MAX_ARG_STRLEN), so any program-internal length limit above that is untestable; nothing suggests one exists.
  - A NUL byte can never appear in argv, so segment content containing 0x00 is unreachable and untested.
  - Flush granularity was inferred from SIGPIPE behavior (exit 141 with `| head -1` for outputs of >= ~3 lines) rather than observed syscall-by-syscall (strace unavailable). For a 12-byte output the SIGPIPE outcome is a race (observed exit 0).
  - Maximum observed segment count is 65526 (limited by the 131071-byte argument cap); behavior of line 5 at values requiring >5 digits (e.g. 100000+) is extrapolated from 1..65526 all printing as plain decimal.
  - Whether the process would report a nonzero status on a write error is settled for /dev/full and closed fd (both exit 0), but other error modes (e.g. EIO mid-write) were not exercised.

YOUR LENS: **exit-codes-and-argc**. Attack the rule specifically from that angle.

Your job is to BREAK IT. Construct inputs where the rule predicts one thing and the binary does another. Actually RUN every candidate counterexample against the binary - never report an unverified counterexample. Focus on: boundaries the rule states (test exactly at, just below, just above), character classes it claims (test every member and every near-miss), interactions with other URL components, and any case the rule is silent about (silence is a defect - if the rule does not say what happens, find out and report it as a correction). Default to skepticism: if the rule is vague enough that two implementers would disagree, that is a 'corrected' verdict with the ambiguity resolved by probe results.

Return verdict 'confirmed' ONLY if you genuinely could not break it after a serious effort (report how many probes you ran in notes). Otherwise 'corrected' (rule mostly right, fix the details) or 'refuted' (fundamentally wrong). Always fill correctedRule with the COMPLETE rule as it should read.

input.correctedRule:
PROGRAM I/O CONTRACT (byte-exact; corrections marked [FIX])

1) ARGUMENT HANDLING  (this section is fully confirmed)
- Let argc be the raw process argument count (including argv[0]).
- if argc < 2: write NOTHING to stdout, NOTHING to stderr, exit status 1.
  * Verified for argc==1 (argv={path,NULL}), argc==1 with an empty argv[0] (argv={"",NULL}), and argc==0
    (execve with argv={NULL}) — all exit 1 with exactly 0 bytes on both streams. argv[1] is never dereferenced,
    so argc==0 does not crash.
  * This path performs no writes at all, so it is immune to every stdout failure mode below: with stdout on an
    already-closed pipe, on /dev/full, or under `ulimit -f 0`, the status is still 1.
- if argc >= 2: use argv[1] verbatim as the URL string. argv[2..] are read by no code and never affect output.
  Verified with 2, 3, 4, 1001, 20001 and 100001 total arguments. The exec-time limit on argument *count* is
  the kernel's total arg+env size cap (~1/4 of RLIMIT_STACK): 400001 args of 8 bytes fails with E2BIG in
  execve, i.e. the program never starts (perl reports "Argument list too long"; bash reports it and exits 126).
- argv[1] == "" is a normal input, NOT the no-arg case: prints "0\n0\n0\n0\n0\n", exit 0. It never falls
  through to a later argument (`binary '' 'http://example.com/a/b'` prints the empty-string output).
- No option parsing whatsoever: "-h", "--help", "--version", "-v", "-", "--", "---" are ordinary URL strings.
- argv is NUL-terminated C strings, so a 0x00 byte can never appear in the input; every other byte 0x01..0xFF
  is accepted verbatim (no validation, transcoding, or locale sensitivity). All 255 single-byte arguments and
  3000 random 1..80-byte binary arguments give exit 0 with 0 bytes of stderr.
- Max deliverable argument is MAX_ARG_STRLEN-1 = 131071 bytes: 131071 works completely (exit 0, full output,
  no truncation); 131072+ is rejected by the kernel with E2BIG before the program runs (execve fails; bash
  prints "Argument list too long" and yields 126). No program-side length limit is observable.
- argv[0] is irrelevant (verified via `exec -a /some/other/name`).

2) STDOUT FORMAT  (confirmed; this is the ENTIRE stdout)
   line 1: is_valid_url(url)       -> one byte '1'(0x31) or '0'(0x30), then LF
   line 2: is_scheme_valid(scheme) -> '1'/'0', LF
   line 3: is_host_valid(host)     -> '1'/'0', LF
   line 4: is_port_valid(port)     -> '1'/'0', LF
   line 5: N = path_segments.size() -> plain unsigned decimal ASCII (no sign, no leading zeros except "0"
                                       itself, no grouping, no padding), LF
   lines 6..5+N: each segment's raw bytes, then LF.
- Numeric bools only (no boolalpha). Separator/terminator is always a single LF; never CR/CRLF, no BOM, no
  padding. A trailing LF is always present; stdout always contains >= 5 LFs and is >= 10 bytes.
- total_bytes = 8 + digits(N) + 1 + sum(len(segment)+1). Verified 10, 12, 14, 16 bytes and 4949 bytes for
  1234×3-char segments; a 65000-segment URL yields N=65000 printed as plain decimal.
- Segments are raw and unescaped: TAB, CR, LF, VT, FF, space, 0x7F and 0x80..0xFF pass through byte for byte;
  no quoting, escaping, percent-decoding or trimming. An LF inside a segment makes physical line count exceed
  5+N. Empty segments are dropped and never printed. A segment never contains '/'.
- [FIX] Output is emitted incrementally, NOT as one write: with stdout on a pipe and an eager reader, a 16-byte
  output arrives in 2 reads (8+8) and a 41-byte output in 3 reads (8+3+30). Combined with the SIGPIPE evidence
  below (the process dies on a pipe closed before it starts, even for the 10-byte minimum output), at least the
  first flush provably happens before the program exits. Exact per-endl syscall granularity is still unverified
  (no strace), but "single atomic write at exit" is refuted.

3) STDERR
- [FIX] "Never written to, for any input" is TRUE only for inputs under a default environment and default
  resource limits. Across ~5400 probes (all 255 single bytes, 3000 random binary strings, 1500 structured
  token-fuzz URLs, ports 2147483648 / 4294967296 / 99999999999999999999 / -2147483649 / 5000 digits, arguments

  * Under a tighter RLIMIT_AS (`ulimit -v 5000`) the dynamic loader fails first and writes

  * The loader also writes to stderr on loader-related env vars (see 5).

- 1   : argc < 2. Nothing written to either stream. Deterministic (100/100).
- 0   : argc >= 2 with a writable stdout — for every input tested, including "", control bytes, invalid UTF-8,

          typically yields 0" claim are both false.
        * `| head -1` is the genuinely racy case: minimal outputs gave 0 in 94/100 and 97/100 runs, larger
          outputs gave 141 ~30-40% of the time. Racy != unreachable, and small != safe.
        * If the parent has SIGPIPE set to SIG_IGN, the program inherits it and never resets it: the identical
          `| true` scenario then exits 0 silently (writes just return EPIPE and are ignored).
        * argc < 2 is never 141 (it writes nothing).
- 153 : SIGXFSZ (128+25) with core dump, when RLIMIT_FSIZE is exceeded while writing to a regular file:
        `ulimit -f 0` + any argc>=2 run -> 153; `ulimit -f 1` + a 65000-segment URL -> 153 after exactly 1024
        bytes reach the file (so partial output plus a fatal signal is observable).
- 134 : SIGABRT with core dump, when memory allocation fails (RLIMIT_AS), stderr carrying the C++ terminate
        message. Not reachable by input alone at the 131071-byte argv cap under default limits.
- 127 : dynamic-loader failure (binary is dynamically linked against libstdc++.so.6, libm.so.6, libgcc_s.so.1,
        libc.so.6 under /opt/compiler/gcc-12/lib). Reachable e.g. under a very small RLIMIT_AS.
- NO EXIT AT ALL: if stdout is a pipe/socket whose reader stalls, the program blocks indefinitely inside its
  write once the 64 KB pipe buffer fills (verified: a ~260 KB output is still running after 3 s with a
  non-reading reader, and completes with exit 0 once the reader drains). There is no timeout, no non-blocking
  write and no error path — so "always exits 0" holds only for a stdout that is actually consumed.
- Consequently, section 1's "argc >= 2 ... exit status 0" must be read as conditional on stdout being writable
  (or silently failing), not truncating, and consumed.

5) NON-INFLUENCES
- stdin is never read (piping data, /dev/null, or a closed fd 0 changes nothing).
- Program output is locale-independent: `env -i`, LANG/LC_ALL/LC_NUMERIC = C, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8,
  de_DE.UTF-8, POSIX, invalid_LOCALE give identical bytes; line 5 is never locale-grouped.
- [FIX] "Environment is irrelevant" is false in general, because the process is dynamically linked and the
  loader runs in the same process: LD_DEBUG=all leaves stdout byte-identical (12 bytes) but writes 891 115
  bytes to stderr with exit 0; LD_PRELOAD=/nonexistent.so writes 118 bytes to stderr with exit 0;
  LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/zzz and GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.check=99 are harmless. STDOUT bytes are environment-
  independent in every case tested; stderr and exit status are not.
- argv[0] is irrelevant. Fully deterministic: repeated runs of the same URL produce identical bytes.
- The program emits LF only; CR under a pty is the terminal's ONLCR translation.

RUST-IMPLEMENTABLE PSEUDOCODE
  let args: Vec<OsString> = env::args_os().collect();
  if args.len() < 2 { exit(1); }                      // nothing printed; unreachable-safe for argc==0
  let url: &[u8] = args[1].as_bytes();
  let u = URL::parse(url);
  let segs = split_path(u.path);
  // Emit incrementally, flushing after each line, and do NOT reset the inherited SIGPIPE disposition
  // (i.e. keep the default fatal action, as C++ does) if you want byte-for-byte status compatibility:
  emit_line(if URL::is_valid_url(url) {b"1"} else {b"0"});
  emit_line(if is_scheme_valid(u.scheme) {b"1"} else {b"0"});
  emit_line(if is_host_valid(u.host)     {b"1"} else {b"0"});
  emit_line(if is_port_valid(u.port)     {b"1"} else {b"0"});
  emit_line(format!("{}", segs.len()).as_bytes());     // usize, plain decimal
  for s in &segs { emit_line(s); }                     // raw bytes
  // emit_line = write_all + flush; write errors are IGNORED (never checked, never reported); blocking writes
  // are allowed to block; fatal SIGPIPE/SIGXFSZ from the kernel are what produce statuses 141/153.
  exit(0);
input.notes:
Ran ~5,400 probes total (255 single-byte args, 3000 random binary args, 1500 structured token-fuzz URLs, 400+ SIGPIPE repetitions, plus targeted exec/rlimit/fd experiments). Built three C helpers under /workspace/probe (/workspace/probe/h.c for custom-argv execve and pre-closed/closed fds, /workspace/probe/h2.c for pipe read-granularity, /workspace/probe/blk.c for a stalled reader) because bash cannot produce argc==0 or a pre-closed stdout pipe.

WHAT SURVIVED: the entire argc contract. argc==0 (argv={NULL}), argc==1, and argv={""} all exit 1 with exactly zero bytes on both streams — argv[1] is never dereferenced. argv[2..] provably unused up to 100001 args. Empty argv[1] is a normal input. No option parsing. 131071-byte argv works, 131072 is a kernel E2BIG. Stdout byte format, the byte-count formula, raw segment emission, and empty-segment dropping all held. No input under default limits produced a nonzero exit or a single byte of stderr — including 5000-digit ports (std::stoi out_of_range is genuinely caught) and 65000-segment paths.

WHAT BROKE (all in the exit-code half of the rule):
1. The SIGPIPE model is wrong in kind, not just in degree. The rule ties 141 to output size ("reachable for outputs of >= ~3 lines", "a 12-byte output typically finishes first and yields 0 (race)"). Reality: with the read end closed before the first write, 141 is deterministic at EVERY size — 100/100 for the exact 12-byte output the rule names, and 141 even for the 10-byte minimum and for argv[1]=="". `| head -1` is the only racy variant. Conversely, an inherited SIGPIPE=SIG_IGN turns the same `| true` pipeline into exit 0, which the rule does not contemplate at all.
2. Two undocumented exit statuses: 153 (SIGXFSZ under `ulimit -f 0`/`-f 1`, with partial output already in the file) and 134 (SIGABRT from an uncaught std::bad_alloc under RLIMIT_AS), plus 127 from loader failure. The rule's list {0,1,141} is presented as exhaustive.
3. "STDERR never written to, for any input" and "no 'terminate called ...' message, no SIGABRT/exit 134 ever observed" are directly falsified: `ulimit -v 9000` on a 65000-segment URL gives exit 134 with 90 bytes of "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_alloc'". This also settles a real implementation fact the rule got backwards — stoi exceptions are caught, allocation failures are not.
4. "Environment is irrelevant" is false for stderr/status: the binary is dynamically linked, so LD_DEBUG=all yields 891 KB of stderr (stdout untouched) and a bad LD_PRELOAD yields 118 bytes. Stdout bytes did remain environment-invariant everywhere.
5. Silence found: the program can block forever (no exit status) when a pipe reader stalls and the 64 KB buffer fills. Section 1's unconditional "argc >= 2 ... exit status 0" also contradicts the rule's own section 4.

Resolved flagged uncertainties: flush granularity is provably incremental (16-byte output arrives in two reads of 8; a pre-closed pipe kills even the minimum output), so "one write at exit" is out, though exact per-endl syscalls remain unconfirmed without strace. Line 5 at >5 digits confirmed at N=65000. NUL-in-segment remains unreachable. Verdict is 'corrected' rather than 'refuted' because the argc/stdout core is accurate and the failures are confined to the exit-status and stderr enumeration.
